title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool to make social-engineering fraud more convincing, not a failure of a deployed AI product. Scammers generated personalized, contextually aware emails impersonating named public figures, using language a cybersecurity expert described as bearing signs of AI generation. The personalization, meaning the references to each recipient's specific work and tailored interview topics, is what made these messages more credible than traditional mass-phishing attempts. The failure point is upstream of any single AI system: the technology that produces fluent, individualized text is being repurposed by external actors, not malfunctioning within a legitimate deployment.

The scam succeeded in at least some cases long enough for recipients to begin engaging before noticing inconsistencies, such as the implausibility of a high-profile host personally handling bookings, or the request for payment. Detection in these cases depended entirely on the recipient's own judgment and willingness to call the organization directly. No automated or institutional check caught the fraud before it reached targets.

Whether any specific AI product or platform was used to generate the emails is not established by the reporting. The reporting also does not identify the perpetrators, and the investigations by WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement had not produced findings at the time of publication.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers have been sending fraudulent emails impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members from WHYY's "Fresh Air" program to authors, entertainers and public figures. The personalized messages reference the recipient's work and propose interview topics, creating a convincing booking process. Eventually, the scammers request payment, typically $250, for supposed production costs. Historian Jennifer Black received such an email and initially became excited before noticing red flags like the request coming directly from Gross herself and suspicious AI-generated language. She called WHYY to verify and confirmed it was a scam.

Similar fraudulent emails have been sent impersonating other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler and journalist Katie Couric. Cybersecurity expert Aunshul Rege explains that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams more convincing and personalized than traditional mass fraud attempts. WHYY and NPR are investigating with law enforcement and have clarified they never charge guests for interviews. Rege advises recipients to watch for red flags like payment requests and to verify invitations through legitimate contact information rather than responding to suspicious messages.
